passed.title: `Expr.cast` raises by default; `strict=False` silently turns bad values into nulls
passed.trap: `Expr.cast` defaults to `strict=True`, so one unparsable string or one out-of-range integer makes the whole query raise. Passing `strict=False` turns every invalid value into null without any warning, so bad data can disappear quietly. Check `Expr.null_count` after a non-strict cast. Integer overflow counts as invalid by default; pass `wrap_numerical=True` only if you really want overflowing values to wrap around.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["1", "2", "x"], "n": [10, 200, 300]})
try:
    df.select(pl.col("s").cast(pl.Int64))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))
loose = df.select(pl.col("s").cast(pl.Int64, strict=False))
print(loose.to_dict(as_series=False))
print(loose.select(pl.col("s").null_count()).item())
try:
    df.select(pl.col("n").cast(pl.UInt8))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))
wrapped = df.select(pl.col("n").cast(pl.UInt8, wrap_numerical=True))
print(wrapped.to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: `Expr.all` and `Expr.any` ignore nulls unless `ignore_nulls=False`
passed.trap: By default (`ignore_nulls=True`), nulls are skipped. A Boolean column like `[null, true]` reports `Expr.all` as `true`, and `[null, false]` reports `Expr.any` as `false`. A column with no non-null values gives `true` for `Expr.all` and `false` for `Expr.any`. If a null should mean "unknown", pass `ignore_nulls=False` to get Kleene logic, which returns null in those cases. Do not confuse `Expr.all` with `pl.all`, which selects every column.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"c": [None, True], "d": [None, False]})
out = df.select(
    all_default=pl.col("c").all(),
    all_kleene=pl.col("c").all(ignore_nulls=False),
    any_default=pl.col("d").any(),
    any_kleene=pl.col("d").any(ignore_nulls=False),
)
print(out.to_dicts())

passed.title: Combine conditions with `&` or `Expr.and_`, never Python `and`, and remember integers go bitwise
passed.trap: Python's `and` keyword asks for the truth value of an expression, and that raises a `TypeError`. Combine predicates with `&` or with `Expr.and_`, and wrap each comparison in parentheses. On integer columns, `&` and `Expr.and_` do a bitwise AND rather than a logical one; for example, `5` AND `-9` is `5`. Make sure both operands are Boolean comparisons when you mean a logical test.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [5, 6, 7], "z": [-9, 2, 7]})
try:
    df.filter(pl.col("x") > 5 and pl.col("z") > 0)
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))
print(df.filter((pl.col("x") > 5) & (pl.col("z") > 0)).rows())
print(df.filter((pl.col("x") > 5).and_(pl.col("z") > 0)).rows())
print(df.select(bitwise=pl.col("x").and_(pl.col("z"))).to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: `Expr.arg_sort` puts nulls first by default
passed.trap: `Expr.arg_sort` defaults to `nulls_last=False`, so the positions of null values come before everything else, even when `descending=True`. Code that assumes the first position points at the smallest (or largest) value will pick a null row instead. Pass `nulls_last=True` when you use `Expr.arg_sort` with `Expr.gather` to reorder or select rows.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"v": [3, None, 1], "name": ["a", "b", "c"]})
print(df.select(pl.col("v").arg_sort()).to_dict(as_series=False))
print(df.select(pl.col("v").arg_sort(nulls_last=True)).to_dict(as_series=False))
first = df.select(pl.col("name").gather(pl.col("v").arg_sort(descending=True)))
print(first.to_dict(as_series=False))
fixed = df.select(
    pl.col("name").gather(pl.col("v").arg_sort(descending=True, nulls_last=True))
)
print(fixed.to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: `Expr.arg_max` and `Expr.arg_min` return a 0-based position, not an index label
passed.trap: Polars has no index, so `Expr.arg_max` and `Expr.arg_min` return an integer row position, not a label. Inside `DataFrame.group_by` aggregations, the position is counted within each group, not across the whole frame. To fetch the matching value from another column, pass the position to `Expr.gather`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"city": ["A", "B", "C"], "temp": [20, 30, 10]})
pos = df.select(pl.col("temp").arg_max(), argmin=pl.col("temp").arg_min())
print(pos.to_dict(as_series=False))
names = df.select(
    hottest=pl.col("city").gather(pl.col("temp").arg_max()),
    coldest=pl.col("city").gather(pl.col("temp").arg_min()),
)
print(names.to_dict(as_series=False))
g = pl.DataFrame({"k": ["x", "x", "y", "y"], "v": [1, 5, 7, 2]})
per_group = g.group_by("k", maintain_order=True).agg(pl.col("v").arg_max())
print(per_group.to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: `Expr.bottom_k` output is unordered and never prefers nulls
passed.trap: `Expr.bottom_k` and `Expr.bottom_k_by` (like `Expr.top_k`) do not guarantee any order in their output, so chain `Expr.sort` if you need the result ordered. They always prefer non-null elements over nulls. `Expr.sort` followed by `Expr.head` behaves differently: it puts nulls first by default, so the two approaches can return different values.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"value": [1, 98, None, 2, 3, 99, 4]})
print(df.select(pl.col("value").bottom_k(3).sort()).to_dict(as_series=False))
print(df.select(pl.col("value").sort().head(3)).to_dict(as_series=False))
top = df.select(pl.col("value").top_k(3).sort(descending=True))
print(top.to_dict(as_series=False))
df2 = pl.DataFrame({"a": [3, 1, 2], "b": ["x", "y", "z"]})
print(df2.select(pl.col("b").bottom_k_by("a", 2).sort()).to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: `Expr.arg_true` changes the row count and cannot be added as a column
passed.trap: `Expr.arg_true` returns only the positions where the condition is true, so its length usually differs from the frame's height. Putting it in `DataFrame.with_columns`, or next to other full-length expressions, raises an error. Use it on its own in `DataFrame.select`. To keep row positions alongside the data, use `DataFrame.with_row_index` followed by `DataFrame.filter`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 1, 2, 1]})
try:
    df.with_columns(idx=(pl.col("a") == 1).arg_true())
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))
out = df.select((pl.col("a") == 1).arg_true().alias("idx"))
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))
kept = df.with_row_index().filter(pl.col("a") == 1)
print(kept.to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: `Expr.agg_groups` is deprecated: aggregate a row index instead
passed.trap: `Expr.agg_groups` is deprecated since 1.35, will be removed in Polars 2.0, and should only be used in an aggregation context. The documented replacement is `df.with_row_index().group_by(...).agg(pl.col("index"))`, which produces the same per-group lists of row positions. Call `DataFrame.with_row_index` before any filtering if you want the original row numbers. The docstring's recommended form passes `maintain_order=True` to `DataFrame.group_by`; do the same if the order of the groups matters.
